Memory.value: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory
My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together
My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things

Negative Appraisals.value: I will not be able to control my anger and will do something terrible
I have permanently changed for the worse
I can't stop bad things from happening to me

vignette: At fourteen, Malik's home life fractured into sudden, violent episodes when his father's frustration turned physical. He never knew which evening would end in shattered glass or a raised hand, only that the atmosphere would curdle without warning. The violence was never explained, only endured, leaving him with a terrifying sense that chaos could descend at any moment. Now, decades later, he struggles to deliberately recall the specific nights, finding the memories stubbornly locked away, yet what he can piece together arrives in disconnected flashes: a shadow looming over the kitchen table, the sharp crack of a belt, the cold floor against his cheek. These fragments feel more real and vivid than ordinary recollections, pressing against his skin like the original terror. The past refuses to stay buried, resurfacing the moment he encounters old photographs or walks into completely unpredictable situations. Last Tuesday, an accidental swipe while organizing his office desk pulled up a picture of his father laughing at a family reunion, and the image instantly fractured into the violent reality behind it, forcing the broken pieces of the past to flood his mind. When the thermostat clicks or a staff member changes their routine without warning at the school, those same disjointed memories surge forward, unbidden and overwhelming. The external cues directly pull the buried recollections to the surface, leaving him little time to brace himself. Because these recollections carry the visceral weight of lived trauma rather than distant history, they cement his conviction that he has been permanently altered for the worse. He watches his own hands while addressing his administrative team, certain that the same volatile current running through his ancestors now courses through him. The sheer reality of those fractured moments convinces him that he can never stop bad things from happening to himself or those he cares for, locking him into a state of quiet desperation. The way the memories feel so undeniably present directly forges his bleak outlook on his own character and safety. The terror of losing control takes hold whenever a routine shifts or a familiar face changes their tone, feeding directly into his dread that he will snap and commit something terrible. When a board member interrupts a staff meeting or his girlfriend leaves her phone ringing unanswered, the fear of his own rage ignites, painting the situation as a prelude to disaster. He has come to believe that every unpredictable encounter is a test he will inevitably fail, eroding his confidence with every passing day. The sudden external shifts directly trigger his deepest fears about his own emotional stability. His certainty that he is fundamentally broken and powerless shapes how he reconstructs the past, forcing the already disjointed fragments to feel more chaotic and threatening. He no longer sees the childhood abuse as isolated incidents of a struggling parent, but as proof of an inescapable fate. The narrative of permanent damage and inevitable helplessness warps his recall, making the memories seem less like historical data and more like active, circulating warnings. His negative self-view directly distorts the way the past is pieced together, amplifying its threat value. The fear that he will eventually harm his partner or lose his position makes every minor shift in environment feel like a direct threat to his safety. He finds himself flinching at the rustle of paperwork or the sudden ring of the office landline, interpreting neutral sounds as precursors to violence. His dread of his own potential rage acts as a constant magnifying glass, turning ordinary fluctuations in his daily life into high-stakes alarms. His appraisals of inevitable catastrophe directly sharpen his sensitivity to environmental cues. The fractured nature of his recollection leaves gaping holes that he must constantly monitor, drawing his attention back to old photographs and waking moments he wishes to forget. Because he cannot piece together a coherent timeline, he remains trapped in a state of alert, scanning his surroundings for clues that might explain the sudden jolt of waking from a nightmare. The inability to organize the past ensures that the present never feels secure, keeping his eyes constantly fixed on familiar objects that suddenly feel dangerous. The gaps in his memory directly compel him to scan his environment for danger signs. Over months, these loops have tightened around his life, costing him his patience at work and causing him to withdraw from his girlfriend under the guise of needing space. He stopped attending parent-teacher nights because the crowded halls felt like a minefield of potential chaos, and he now sleeps with a flashlight under his pillow, bracing for the moment his dreams turn real. What finally brought him to seek help was a morning when he accidentally slammed his car door too hard and immediately collapsed, terrified that the violence had finally taken root. He is most afraid that he is past the point of repair, but he hopes, with a fragile certainty, that someone might help him untangle the knot before it snaps completely.
